newsitem.title: UK: Sterling debt and futures closing report.
newsitem.headline: Sterling debt and futures closing report.

text.p: Gilts ended a touch higher on Monday with investors facing a whole host of reasons not to dive into the market, dealers said.

On Tuesday, the Federal Open Market Committee may put up U.S. interest rates by a quarter-point. That could signal the turn of the international interest rate cycle, a bitter pill for the bond markets to swallow.
And for gilts, an auction of 10-year stock on Wednesday will keep trade subdued, as will the Easter holiday starting Friday.
"The auction won't be a problem but I don't expect to see the market rising before it," one gilts salesman said.
"It will be a quiet week anyway with Easter coming up."

Only a paltry 46,000 June gilt future contracts changed hands on Monday. The future settled 4/32 higher at 109-10 which represented something of a come-back having dropped as low as 108-27 earlier in the session.

The market paid little attention to this morning's batch of UK economic data which showed gross domestic product grew by 0.8 percent in the fourth quarter and a current account surplus of 873 million stg.
On Wednesday, the Bank of England will auction 2.5 billion stg of 7.25 percent gilts due 2007 -- the new 10-year benchmark.
Analysts at Merrill Lynch said with no further 10-year supply expected two months or more, the 10-year gilt could outperform the rest of the curve.

But before the auction comes the FOMC. A poll of 48 economists by Reuters showed 34 expected the Fed to raise its federal funds target to at least 5.50 percent on Tuesday from 5.25 percent. With bond markets ready for a rate rise, they could even rally for a while. But not for too long. "One's really hard pressed to say a Fed rate hike is positive for global bonds," said George Magnus, chief international economist at UBS.
"It may be for a day or two but the fundamentals that are giving rise to this Fed rate hike are actually causing sentiment in Japan and Europe to turn," he added.
The gilt/Bund spread, which was at 182 basis points late last week, edged out to 184 on Monday.
"The domestics aren't really involved at the moment. Everyone is holding back in case the U.S. does anything tomorrow and with the auction on Wednesday," one gilt dealer said.
June short sterling futures settled unchanged at 93.32 on Monday, pricing in a half-point UK interest rate rise by the end of the first half.
Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets, said Monday's robust GDP numbers reaffirmed the likelihood of a rate rise after the May Day election.
"These numbers provide further evidence of the robust background to growth this year," he said. "We expect base rates to rise by a 1/4 point shortly after the poll."
